name: Finite element method (FEM)
domain: 车辆—轨道与基础结构动力学
definition_zh: 将连续域划分为有限单元，通过单元近似和组装方程求解连续体问题的数值方法。
scope_note: 与有限元模型、有限单元对象和有限元理论区分。
usage_overview: 用于离散钢轨、轨枕、轨道板及桥梁、路基和土体，组装质量、阻尼和刚度矩阵并建立结构或耦合系统方程；也常作为其他离散方法与求解算法的数值对照。具体单元类型和结构假设由所分析的构件决定。

complete_examples.text: The slab track system is modeled by finite element method (FEM), and can be decomposed into track segment elements (TSEs) [28].

For example, when the tracks are modelled by finite element method (FEM), the track participated in train-track interactions can reach hundreds of meters or even kilometres, and accordingly the degrees of freedom (D.O.F.) of the system in time integration process might be very large.
This approach is based on the finite element method (FEM) and draws essence from wheel-rail coupling model [27] to accurately characterize the wheel-rail contact geometries/creepages.
Terefore, we will meticulously construct their dynamic matrices using finite element method (FEM).

Instead of the expensive full-scale experiments, an alter-native, a combination of discrete element method (DEM) and finite element method (FEM) to model the ballasted track system, is therefore developed to obtain sufficiently enough track properties to achieve statistical evaluation of uneven track parameters.

In the numerical simulation research presented above, abundant and fairly practical work has been accomplished, in which the finite element method (FEM) is widely applied to realize track dynamics analysis [8-13, 16, 18-19] but mostly with the assistance of commercial software such as ANSYS and ABAQUS, etc.

Recently Xu and Zhai [31] made an extensive research on vehicle–track stochastic dynamics, in which the longitudinal randomness of the track was modelled by finite element method (FEM), and solved by time-domain integral schemes.

Railway system Vehicle-track-subgrade interaction finite element method wheel-rail contacts a b s t r a c t In this work a three-dimensional vehicle-ballasted track-subgrade interaction model is developed, where the vehicle is modeled as a multi-rigid-body system, the track-subgrade interaction is modelled by finite element method (FEM) with the rail modelled as beam elements, the sleeper and the subgrade layers modelled as solid elements, and the vehicle and the track-subgrade system are coupled by unified matrix formulations and solved simultaneously and time-dependently.

In the aforementioned work a wide variety of models are developed for solving different problems, besides the method-ologies, such as multi-body dynamics, finite element method (FEM), boundary element method, etc.
The vehicle and track can be defined by general schemes such as multi-rigid-body dynamics and finite element method (FEM).

Aiming at the aforementioned issues, this work con-tributes to developing a more complex VTT dynamic model by coupling the vehicle, the track and the tunnel as an entire system, where the track-tunnel system is modeled by the finite element method (FEM) and the soil around the tunnel is modeled by the infinite element method (IEM).

In the previous work, there are mainly two types of track-soil prediction models serving the research: analytical method and numerical method, in which the numerical method includes finite element method (FEM) and boundary element method (BEM).
Considering the parametric and geometric non-uniformity, nonlinearity, and the modelling efficiency, finite element method (FEM) is generally a more useful tool for track-bridge interaction analysis.

Its direct implementation on train-structure interaction modeled by finite element method (FEM), especially for models with high degrees of freedom (DoFs) and consistent mass matrices, shows limitations in solution stability and efficiency.
Herein, they are simulated as elastic bodies by applying the Finite Element Method (FEM).
A substructure coordination method is proposed based on the vehicle–track–soil finite element method (FEM) and differential quadrature finite element method (DQFEM) coupled dynamic model.
In the 3D track model, the modal superposition method (MSM) [1, 2, 16–18] and finite element method (FEM) [19–21] are adopted mostly.

Contrary to that, numerical tech niques such as Finite Element Method (FEM) [25], Boundary Element Method (BEM) [26] and hybrid FEM-BEM [27] have become highly effective tools for modelling the complex train-track-bridge interaction problem.
